parts.context: Freya, who is working from home today, phones Dan at IT support.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: Hi Dan, it's Freya. I'm working from home today, and I'm having problems with my video calls. The picture keeps freezing, and people can't hear me properly.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: OK. Are you using the wi-fi or a cable?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: The wi-fi. The router is downstairs, and I'm sitting in my bedroom upstairs.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: That's probably the problem. Wi-fi signals get weaker if they go through walls and floors. Can you move closer to the router?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: Not really. My children are watching TV in the living room, right next to it.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: I see. Is anyone else using the internet at the moment?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: Yes, I think my son is playing an online game.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: That uses a lot of bandwidth. If he stops the game during your call, the picture will be much better. Another option is a powerline adapter. It sends the internet signal through the electrical wires in your house, so you get a wired connection upstairs.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: That sounds good. Where can I get one?

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: We keep some in the IT office. If you come in tomorrow, I'll give you one.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: Great. For now, I'll ask my son to stop playing. Thanks, Dan.

parts.context: Laura presents a short technology programme about a new mobile app for train passengers.

script.speaker: Laura
script.text: Welcome to Tech Today. I'm Laura. This week, the national rail company is introducing its new mobile app, RailGo, and lots of passengers are already using it. Here's what it does.

script.speaker: Laura
script.text: First, you can buy tickets on the app, and the ticket appears as a QR code on your phone. If you show the code at the gate, the gate opens automatically, so you don't need a paper ticket.

script.speaker: Laura
script.text: Second, the app shows live train times. If your train is late, the app sends you a message straight away. It also tells you which platform your train is leaving from.

script.speaker: Laura
script.text: Third, the app uses your location to find the nearest station. This is very useful when you're visiting a new city.

script.speaker: Laura
script.text: The app is free, and it works on both Android and Apple phones. It needs about 80 megabytes of space. One warning, though: the app uses GPS a lot, so it can reduce your battery life. If you're going on a long journey, take a charger with you. That's all for today.

passage.title: Less Email, More Work
paragraphs: Two years ago, staff at Brightline Insurance in Bristol were receiving about 120 emails a day. Many of these messages were copies of conversations which did not really concern them. A survey showed that employees spent nearly three hours a day reading and answering email, and many people were checking their inbox late at night.

The company's managers decided to make some changes. First, they introduced a chat app for short questions. If someone needs a quick answer, they now send a chat message instead of an email. Email is only for longer messages and for messages that go to customers.

Second, staff stopped copying the whole team on every message. Now they only send an email to the people who need to do something about it. Third, the company's email server holds messages that are sent after seven in the evening and delivers them the next morning at eight. Managers can still send urgent messages at night, but they have to mark them as urgent.

The results are impressive. Staff now receive about forty emails a day, and they spend about one hour a day on email. In a second survey, 80 per cent of employees said that they felt less stressed. However, some staff say that the chat app is now becoming a problem, because it sends them a notification every few minutes. The company is considering a quiet hour every afternoon, when nobody can send chat messages.

passage.title: Browse Safely: Five Simple Tips
paragraphs: 1. Look at the address bar. If a website address starts with https, the connection between your browser and the website is encrypted. Never type your card details on a page whose address only starts with http.
2. Keep your browser up to date. Most browsers update themselves automatically, but if yours asks you to restart it, do it as soon as possible.
3. Be careful with pop-up windows. If a pop-up says that your computer has a virus, close it. Real antivirus programs do not warn you in a browser window.

4. Use private browsing on shared computers. If you use a private window, the browser does not save your history or your passwords when you close it. However, private browsing does not hide what you do from your employer or your internet provider.
5. Clear your browsing data from time to time. This removes old cookies, which are small files that websites use to remember you. You will need to log in to some websites again afterwards.

Relative clauses with which, that or who: 'Accounts', which lists all your accounts
Zero or first conditional: If the phone asks for a server address, type… / it will…

email.modelAnswer:
From: Nguyen Duc Long
To: Ellie
Date: 6th February
Subject: Work email on your new phone

Hi Ellie,

We're moving to a new email system this month.
It should be quite easy to set up your work email on your phone.
First, open Settings and select 'Accounts', which lists all your accounts.
Then, tap 'Add account' and choose 'Exchange'.
Next, enter your work email address and password.
After that, choose what to sync: email, calendar and contacts.
Finally, if the phone asks for a server address, just type mail.brightway.com.
Don't forget to delete the old email account when you've finished.

Best wishes,
Nguyen Duc Long
IT Officer
IT Department

parts.instructions: Explain some email terms. Speak for 1–1.5 minutes.
parts.prompt: A new colleague has never used email at work. Explain what each part of an email in the cues is and why it is useful. Use relative clauses with which, that or who (The recipient is the person who…, An attachment is a file which…).
requiredGrammar: Relative clauses with which, that or who: The recipient is the person who…, An attachment is a file which…
parts.sampleAnswer: Let me explain the main parts of an email. The subject line is the short line at the top which tells people what the email is about. You should always write a clear one. The recipient is the person who receives your email, so you type their address in the 'To' box. A copy, or cc, is for people who need to know about the message but don't need to reply. An attachment is a file that you send with the email, for example a report or a photo. Be careful with large attachments, because some servers don't accept them. Finally, the signature is the text which appears at the end of every email. It shows your name, your job title and your phone number, so customers know how to contact you.

parts.instructions: Deal with the situation. Speak for 1–1.5 minutes.
parts.prompt: You are phoning the IT helpdesk because your web browser is behaving strangely today. Explain what you usually do with the browser and what is happening now. Use the present simple for your normal routine, the present continuous for what is happening at the moment, and state verbs in the simple form (I don't know…, I need…, I want…).
cues: normal routine: open the company intranet every morning / use the browser for online orders
now: the browser is showing a warning message about the intranet
now: pages are loading very slowly / a pop-up window keeps appearing
you don't know if the site is safe / you need the order page for a customer today
requiredGrammar: Present simple for routines: I usually open…, I use…
Present continuous for things happening now: The browser is showing…, Pages are loading…
State verbs in the simple form: I don't know…, I need…, I want…
parts.sampleAnswer: Hi, this is Mai from the sales department. I'm having a problem with my browser today. Normally, I open the company intranet every morning, and I use the browser all day for customers' online orders. It usually works perfectly. But this morning, the browser is showing a strange warning message about the intranet. It says that the connection isn't private. Also, the pages are loading very slowly, and a pop-up window keeps appearing every few minutes. I'm not clicking on anything in the pop-up. I don't know if the intranet is safe at the moment, so I don't want to type my password. The problem is that I need the order page today, because a customer is waiting for a delivery. Could someone check it for me, please?
